newsitem.title: NORWAY: Arafat urges Norway to pressure aid-donor states.
newsitem.headline: Arafat urges Norway to pressure aid-donor states.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat urged Norway on Tuesday to press donor countries to honour aid pledges, so easing critical social conditions in self-ruled Palestinian areas closed off by Israel.

"President Arafat described a quite desperate picture of the situation in the Palestinian areas," Norwegian aid minister Kari Nordheim-Larsen told Reuters after meeting the Palestinian leader on the second day of his official visit.
"The border closures stop people from working and automatically lead to difficult social conditions," she said.
Donor countries had pledged around $2.2 billion to self-ruled Palestinian areas in 1996 but only about half that had so far translated into aid, she said.

Norway, which played a leading role in brokering the peace accord between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation in 1993, chairs the Ad-hoc Liaison Committee of countries donating to Palestinian finances.
"Arafat asked us to use the chairmanship role to go to the other donors and ask why the money has not been put on the table and to convince them of the need for more money," Nordheim-Larsen said.
"This is not new for Norway, but it is crucial for the time being mainly because of the border closures and their immediate impact on social conditions," she said.
Norway pledged and paid $60 million this year and will donate the same amount next year, she said, adding that Arafat had not asked Norway for more aid.

Foreign ministry spokesman Ingvard Havnen said Arafat, in Oslo on the first leg of a European tour, on Monday met new Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland and discussed Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns the Jewish state has agreed to hand over to Palestinian self-rule.
Both the PLO and Isreal have accused each other of foot-dragging on a deal on Israeli troop redeployment from Hebron, key to the pledged partial Israeli withdrawal.
Norway, which has observers in the city, is the only foreign country to monitor relations there.
"We hope parties will reach an agreement on the redeployment of Israeli forces in Hebron before November 12 when the current mandate (for the observers) runs out," Havnen said.
"We have not yet considered what will happen after that."
